subject: geography
description: Geography skill tree, FET Grades 10-12 (CAPS Geography Grades 10-12). Tiers = CAPS topic clusters (≈ terms). Mastery = 60% of a 20-item pool (FET rule, no timer). ALL questions available — no prerequisites between skills, learner chooses any skill in any order. LIGHT-VISUAL build: stimulus is text or inline data tables (data-interpret); the only images are a one-time library of ~12 generic SVG diagrams referenced by image_refs (diagram-label). No sourced 1:50 000 maps, orthophotos or per-question graphs — live-map interpretation is handed to the matric papers section. Mapwork is taught as given-number calculations (choice/scenario) plus map/GIS concepts. Input types reuse existing engine templates: choice, true-false, cloze, scenario, match, sort-buckets, sequence, data-interpret, diagram-label, highlight-source — no new mechanics. Items live in data/geography-question-bank.json. v1.1: ALL THREE GRADES authored — Grade 10 (20 skills), Grade 11 (21 skills), Grade 12 (23 skills) = 64 skills across 15 tiers, 1,280 items. 23 diagram SVGs referenced by image_refs still to be drawn (image gaps). Head-of-ed review pending.

levels.title: Grade 10 — Geography
levels.description: Four CAPS topics plus a cross-cutting mapwork strand. Mapwork & techniques (calculations, GIS concepts). The Atmosphere (composition, heating, moisture, synoptic weather maps). Geomorphology (Earth structure, plate tectonics, folding & faulting, earthquakes, volcanoes). Population (distribution, structure, growth, movement, HIV/AIDS). Water resources (water in the world, oceans, water management in SA, floods). 20 atomic skills, all unlocked, learner-chosen order.

atomic_skills.title: Map calculations
atomic_skills.description: Working out real-world answers from given map values on a 1:50 000 map: scale and the meaning of ratio scale, straight-line and curved distance, gradient (vertical interval ÷ horizontal distance), magnetic bearing and magnetic declination, area, and vertical exaggeration. Every value needed is supplied in the question — no map image required.

error_signatures.description: Confuses the 1:50 000 ratio (1 cm = 0,5 km), e.g. treats 1 cm as 50 km or 5 km
error_signatures.example: Says 4 cm on a 1:50 000 map is 200 km

error_signatures.description: Forgets to convert units before dividing in a gradient calculation
error_signatures.example: Divides vertical interval in metres by horizontal distance in cm

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: On a 1:50 000 map, 1 cm on the map = 0,5 km (500 m) on the ground. Distance: measure cm × 0,5 = km. Gradient: VI ÷ HD with BOTH in metres, written as 1:n. Magnetic bearing = true bearing + magnetic declination. Always convert units to match BEFORE you divide.

atomic_skills.title: Map & GIS concepts
atomic_skills.description: Reading the language of maps without needing a live map: latitude/longitude and how position is given in degrees, minutes and seconds; map symbols and contour basics; the difference between a topographic map, an aerial photograph and an orthophoto map and what each is used for; and the core ideas of GIS — layers, raster vs vector data, remote sensing and why GIS is useful.

error_signatures.description: Cannot distinguish an orthophoto (corrected, to scale) from an ordinary aerial photograph
error_signatures.example: Says you can measure true distance directly off any aerial photo

error_signatures.description: Thinks GIS is just a digital picture of a map rather than layered, queryable data
error_signatures.example: Says GIS and a scanned paper map are the same thing

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: A topographic map is drawn to scale with symbols and contours. An aerial photo is a raw picture (distortion at the edges). An orthophoto is an aerial photo corrected to true scale, so you CAN measure on it. GIS stores information in separate layers you can switch on/off and query — it is data, not just a picture.

atomic_skills.title: Composition & structure of the atmosphere
atomic_skills.description: Why the atmosphere matters; the gases that make it up (mostly nitrogen and oxygen); the four layers — troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere — and how temperature changes through each; the ozone layer in the stratosphere; and the causes, effects of, and ways to reduce ozone depletion.

error_signatures.description: Confuses ozone depletion (stratosphere) with the greenhouse effect / global warming (troposphere)
error_signatures.example: Says the ozone hole is what causes global warming

error_signatures.description: Gets the layer order or their temperature behaviour wrong
error_signatures.example: Says temperature always falls with height through every layer

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Order from the ground up: TROPOsphere (weather, gets colder with height) → STRATOsphere (ozone layer, gets warmer with height) → MESOsphere (coldest) → THERMOsphere (very hot). Ozone depletion is a stratosphere problem (lets in UV); the greenhouse effect is a troposphere problem (traps heat). They are different.

atomic_skills.title: Heating of the atmosphere
atomic_skills.description: How the atmosphere is heated — insolation, reflection, scattering, absorption, radiation, conduction and convection; the factors that make some places warmer than others (latitude, altitude, ocean currents, distance from the sea); the greenhouse effect and its impact; and global warming — its evidence, causes and consequences for Africa.

error_signatures.description: Thinks the atmosphere is heated mainly directly by the Sun from above rather than from the Earth's surface upward
error_signatures.example: Says air high up is hottest because it is closest to the Sun

error_signatures.description: Cannot explain why altitude lowers temperature
error_signatures.example: Says mountains are cold because they are closer to the Sun

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: The Sun heats the GROUND; the ground then heats the air above it — so air is warmest near the surface and gets colder with altitude (about 6,5 °C per 1 000 m). Four big controls on temperature: LATITUDE (low = hotter), ALTITUDE (high = colder), OCEAN CURRENTS (warm/cold), and DISTANCE FROM SEA (coast = milder).

atomic_skills.title: Moisture in the atmosphere
atomic_skills.description: Water in the air as vapour and liquid; evaporation, condensation and precipitation; dew point, condensation level, humidity and relative humidity; how and why clouds form and what cloud types tell us; forms of precipitation (rain, hail, snow, dew, frost); and the three rainfall types — relief, convectional and frontal.

error_signatures.description: Confuses the three rainfall mechanisms (relief, convectional, frontal)
error_signatures.example: Calls afternoon thunderstorm rain 'relief rainfall'

error_signatures.description: Misunderstands relative humidity as the actual amount of water rather than a percentage of capacity
error_signatures.example: Says 100% humidity means the air is half water

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Air holds water vapour; warm air holds more. Cool air to its DEW POINT and vapour condenses into cloud/dew. Relative humidity = how full the air is, as a % of what it could hold at that temperature. Three rainfalls: RELIEF (air forced up a mountain), CONVECTIONAL (hot ground, rising air, afternoon storms), FRONTAL (warm air rides over cold air at a front).

atomic_skills.title: Reading & interpreting synoptic weather maps
atomic_skills.description: The weather elements shown on a synoptic chart — temperature, dew-point, cloud cover, wind direction and speed, atmospheric pressure; reading station-model data (given as a small table or symbol key, not a sourced chart); and interpreting basic pressure patterns (highs, lows, isobars) and the weather they bring. Atmospheric pressure is introduced here and developed in Grade 11.

error_signatures.description: Reads a station-model wind barb backwards (direction wind blows TO rather than FROM)
error_signatures.example: Says a north wind blows towards the north

error_signatures.description: Confuses high- and low-pressure cells and their weather
error_signatures.example: Says a low brings clear, dry weather

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Wind is named by where it comes FROM (a south wind blows from the south). On a synoptic map, closely-spaced isobars = strong wind. LOW pressure = rising air = cloud and rain; HIGH pressure = sinking air = clear, dry weather. Read each station-model value off the key one at a time.

atomic_skills.title: The structure of the Earth
atomic_skills.description: The internal layers of the Earth — crust (continental and oceanic), mantle, outer core and inner core — and their key features; the difference between continental and oceanic crust; and how heat from the core drives convection currents in the mantle.

error_signatures.description: Reverses the density/thickness of continental vs oceanic crust
error_signatures.example: Says oceanic crust is thicker and lighter than continental crust

error_signatures.description: Does not link mantle convection to the heat of the core
error_signatures.example: Says the mantle moves because of the Moon's gravity

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: From the outside in: CRUST (thin, solid) → MANTLE (hot, slowly flowing rock) → OUTER CORE (liquid iron/nickel) → INNER CORE (solid, hottest). Oceanic crust is THINNER but DENSER; continental crust is THICKER but lighter. Heat from the core makes the mantle churn in convection currents — that movement drags the plates.

atomic_skills.title: Plate tectonics
atomic_skills.description: The theory of plate tectonics and the evidence for it (continental fit, fossils, rock matches); the three plate boundaries — divergent (spreading), convergent (colliding), transform (sliding past) — and the landforms and events each produces; and how mantle convection moves the plates.

error_signatures.description: Mixes up the three boundary types and their results
error_signatures.example: Says plates moving apart cause mountains to fold up

error_signatures.description: Thinks plates float on liquid rather than being dragged by convection
error_signatures.example: Says continents drift because the sea pushes them

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Three boundaries: DIVERGENT (plates move APART — new crust, mid-ocean ridges, rift valleys), CONVERGENT (plates COLLIDE — mountains, ocean trenches, volcanoes), TRANSFORM (plates SLIDE past — earthquakes, e.g. San Andreas). The engine is mantle convection dragging the plates from below.

atomic_skills.title: Folding & faulting
atomic_skills.description: How compression folds rock layers — anticlines (up-folds) and synclines (down-folds) — and the fold mountains this builds; how tension and compression fracture rock along faults — normal, reverse and the landforms like fault scarps, block mountains (horsts) and rift valleys (grabens).

error_signatures.description: Swaps anticline and syncline
error_signatures.example: Calls a down-fold an anticline

error_signatures.description: Confuses folding (bending) with faulting (breaking)
error_signatures.example: Says a fault is a bend in rock layers

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: FOLDING = rock BENDS under compression: anticline = arch (up), syncline = trough (down). FAULTING = rock BREAKS and moves along a crack: a raised block between two faults is a horst (block mountain); a dropped block is a graben (rift valley). Folds bend, faults break.

atomic_skills.title: Earthquakes
atomic_skills.description: What causes earthquakes (sudden release of stress along faults); focus and epicentre; measuring magnitude and intensity; where earthquakes happen and why; their effects on people and the environment; and how people prepare for and respond to them.

error_signatures.description: Confuses focus (underground origin) with epicentre (point on the surface above it)
error_signatures.example: Says the epicentre is deep underground

error_signatures.description: Thinks magnitude and intensity are the same thing
error_signatures.example: Says a high magnitude always means the most damage everywhere

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: The FOCUS is where the rock slips underground; the EPICENTRE is the point on the surface directly above it. MAGNITUDE = energy released (one number, e.g. Richter); INTENSITY = how much shaking/damage is felt at a place (varies with distance, ground and buildings). Most quakes happen along plate boundaries.

atomic_skills.title: Volcanoes
atomic_skills.description: How volcanoes form and erupt; the parts of a volcano (magma chamber, vent, crater); types of volcanic activity and landforms; where volcanoes occur and why (plate boundaries and hotspots); and the negative and positive effects of volcanoes on people and the environment.

error_signatures.description: Uses magma and lava interchangeably
error_signatures.example: Says magma flows down the outside of the volcano

error_signatures.description: Sees volcanoes as only harmful, missing benefits
error_signatures.example: Says volcanoes have no positive effects at all

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: MAGMA is molten rock UNDERGROUND; once it erupts onto the surface it is LAVA. Volcanoes cluster at plate boundaries and hotspots. They are dangerous (ash, lava, gases, lahars) BUT also bring benefits: very fertile soils, geothermal energy, minerals and tourism.

atomic_skills.title: Population distribution & density
atomic_skills.description: The difference between distribution (where people are) and density (how crowded, people per km²); how to calculate population density; the physical and human factors that draw people to or push them from an area; and reading population distribution from a choropleth-style data table.

error_signatures.description: Uses 'distribution' and 'density' as if identical
error_signatures.example: Says a country with high density must have an even distribution

error_signatures.description: Calculates density without dividing by area
error_signatures.example: Calls the total population the density

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: DISTRIBUTION = the PATTERN of where people live (even, clustered, sparse). DENSITY = a NUMBER: total people ÷ area in km². High density spots are pulled by water, flat land, good climate, jobs and cities; deserts, mountains and dense forest are sparse.

atomic_skills.title: Population structure
atomic_skills.description: Reading a population pyramid — age and sex structure; the shapes of expansive (wide-base), constrictive and stationary pyramids and what they tell us; dependency ratio; and what a country's structure implies for its future and its services.

error_signatures.description: Cannot link pyramid shape to growth rate
error_signatures.example: Says a wide-based pyramid means a shrinking population

error_signatures.description: Misreads which sex/age the two sides and bars represent
error_signatures.example: Reads the longest bar as the oldest age group

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: A population pyramid stacks age groups (youngest at the bottom) with males on one side, females on the other. WIDE base = many children = fast-growing (expansive). Narrowing base = slowing growth (constrictive). Straight sides = stable (stationary). A wide base means lots of dependents to feed, school and care for.

atomic_skills.title: Population growth
atomic_skills.description: Birth rate, death rate and natural increase; how to calculate natural increase and growth rate; the demographic transition model in plain terms; factors that change birth and death rates; and world case studies of fast- and slow-growing populations.

error_signatures.description: Calculates natural increase by adding birth and death rates instead of subtracting
error_signatures.example: Adds birth rate and death rate to get growth

error_signatures.description: Thinks population can only grow through births, ignoring migration in total change
error_signatures.example: Says natural increase already includes migration

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: NATURAL INCREASE = birth rate − death rate (per 1 000 people), then ÷10 for a %. It does NOT include migration — that is added separately for TOTAL change. As countries develop, death rates fall first (better health), then birth rates fall later, so growth is fast in between and slow at the end.

atomic_skills.title: Population movements
atomic_skills.description: Migration concepts — emigration, immigration, internal vs international, voluntary vs forced; push and pull factors; rural-to-urban migration and urbanisation; and the effects of migration on both the source and the destination area, with case studies.

error_signatures.description: Swaps emigration (leaving) and immigration (arriving)
error_signatures.example: Says someone emigrates INTO a country

error_signatures.description: Mislabels push and pull factors
error_signatures.example: Calls 'better jobs in the city' a push factor

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: EMIGRATE = Exit (leave a country); IMMIGRATE = come In. PUSH factors drive people AWAY from where they are (drought, war, no jobs); PULL factors attract them to a new place (jobs, safety, services). Most internal migration in developing countries is rural → urban, driving urbanisation.

atomic_skills.title: HIV and AIDS
atomic_skills.description: The difference between HIV and AIDS; how the pandemic affects population structure, life expectancy, the workforce and dependency; its social and economic impact with reference to Africa; and prevention, treatment and management strategies.

error_signatures.description: Treats HIV and AIDS as the same thing
error_signatures.example: Says everyone with HIV has AIDS

error_signatures.description: Cannot connect the pandemic to changes in population structure
error_signatures.example: Says HIV/AIDS has no effect on a population pyramid

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: HIV is the VIRUS; AIDS is the advanced STAGE of illness it can cause if untreated. A heavy HIV/AIDS burden removes many working-age adults, lowering life expectancy, leaving orphans, and shrinking the middle of the population pyramid. Treatment (ARVs), education and prevention reduce the impact.

atomic_skills.title: Water in the world
atomic_skills.description: The water cycle and its processes; the distribution of fresh and salt water and why fresh water is scarce; the value of water as a resource; and the idea of water as a shared, finite resource under pressure.

error_signatures.description: Overestimates how much of Earth's water is fresh and usable
error_signatures.example: Says most of the planet's water is drinkable fresh water

error_signatures.description: Confuses water-cycle processes (evaporation, condensation, precipitation, transpiration)
error_signatures.example: Calls cloud formation 'precipitation'

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Almost all Earth's water (about 97%) is salt water in the oceans; only ~3% is fresh, and most of that is locked in ice and groundwater — so usable fresh water is tiny and precious. Water cycle order: EVAPORATION → CONDENSATION (clouds) → PRECIPITATION → runoff/infiltration → back to the sea.

atomic_skills.title: The world's oceans
atomic_skills.description: The oceans as part of the global system; ocean currents — warm and cold — and how they affect the climate of nearby coasts; the Benguela (cold) and Agulhas (warm) currents around South Africa; and the importance of oceans to people.

error_signatures.description: Swaps which SA current is warm and which is cold
error_signatures.example: Says the Benguela on the west coast is warm

error_signatures.description: Cannot link a cold current to a dry coast and a warm current to a wetter coast
error_signatures.example: Says the cold west coast is wetter than the warm east coast

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Around South Africa: the BENGUELA current (WEST coast) is COLD → dry air, little rain, west coast is arid. The AGULHAS current (EAST coast) is WARM → moist air, more rain, lush east coast. Warm currents warm and wet the coast they pass; cold currents cool and dry it.

atomic_skills.title: Water management in South Africa
atomic_skills.description: South Africa as a water-scarce country; where our water comes from (rivers, dams, groundwater, inter-basin transfers); the causes of water shortages; and strategies to manage and conserve water at home, in farming and in industry.

error_signatures.description: Assumes South Africa has plentiful water
error_signatures.example: Says South Africa gets more rain than the world average

error_signatures.description: Cannot match a water problem to a sensible management strategy
error_signatures.example: Says building more lawns saves water

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: South Africa is a WATER-SCARCE country: rainfall is low (about half the world average) and unevenly spread. We rely on dams, rivers, groundwater and inter-basin transfers (moving water between catchments). Manage demand by saving water, fixing leaks, drip irrigation, recycling and protecting catchments.

atomic_skills.title: Floods
atomic_skills.description: What causes floods (heavy or prolonged rain, snowmelt, dam failure, poor drainage); the difference between natural and human contributing factors; the effects of floods on people, property and the environment; and ways to reduce flood risk and respond to floods.

error_signatures.description: Sees floods as purely natural, ignoring human causes like building on floodplains
error_signatures.example: Says people can never make a flood worse

error_signatures.description: Confuses flood causes with flood effects
error_signatures.example: Lists 'heavy rain' as an effect of a flood

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: CAUSES of floods: heavy/long rain, snowmelt, dam failure — made worse by HUMAN actions (clearing vegetation, hard paved surfaces, building on floodplains, blocked drains). EFFECTS: lost lives, damaged homes and crops, disease, eroded soil. Reduce risk with drainage, wetlands, flood barriers, warnings and zoning.

levels.title: Grade 11 — Geography
levels.description: Four CAPS topics plus the mapwork strand. The Atmosphere (energy balance, global air circulation, Africa's weather & climate, droughts & desertification). Geomorphology (topography of horizontal, inclined and igneous rocks, slopes, mass movements). Development geography (concept, frameworks, trade, issues, aid). Resources & sustainability (using resources, soil erosion, conventional & non-conventional energy, energy management). 21 atomic skills, all unlocked, learner-chosen order.

atomic_skills.title: Topographic map techniques (cross-sections, gradient, intervisibility)
atomic_skills.description: Applying 1:50 000 map skills with given values: matching contours to landforms, building and reading cross-sections, calculating vertical exaggeration, working out gradient, judging intervisibility (can two points see each other), and calculating area — all from numbers supplied in the question.

error_signatures.description: Computes vertical exaggeration with the scales the wrong way up
error_signatures.example: Divides horizontal scale by vertical scale

error_signatures.description: Thinks a hidden valley between two hills does not affect intervisibility
error_signatures.example: Says two hilltops are always intervisible regardless of land between

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Vertical exaggeration = vertical scale ÷ horizontal scale. Gradient = VI ÷ HD (both in metres) as 1:n. Intervisibility: draw the cross-section — if higher ground or a hill rises into the line of sight between two points, they CANNOT see each other.

atomic_skills.title: Aerial photos, orthophotos & GIS data
atomic_skills.description: Interpreting oblique vs vertical aerial photographs using tone, texture and shadow; identifying features on orthophoto maps and orienting them to a topographic map; and GIS data ideas — spatially referenced data, spatial vs spectral resolution, data types (point, line, area, attribute) and raster vs vector.

error_signatures.description: Confuses oblique and vertical aerial photographs
error_signatures.example: Says a vertical photo shows the sides of buildings

error_signatures.description: Mixes up spatial resolution (pixel size) with spectral resolution (wavelength bands)
error_signatures.example: Says higher spatial resolution means more colour bands

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Vertical photo = straight down (like a map, only tops visible); oblique = at an angle (sides visible, gives a 3-D feel). On photos use TONE (light/dark), TEXTURE (smooth/rough) and SHADOW to identify features. Spatial resolution = how small a pixel covers on the ground; spectral resolution = how many wavelength bands are sensed.

atomic_skills.title: The Earth's energy balance
atomic_skills.description: The unequal heating of the atmosphere by latitude and season; the significance of the Earth's tilted axis and its revolution around the Sun; and how energy is transferred and balanced around the planet by ocean currents and winds.

error_signatures.description: Thinks seasons are caused by the Earth being closer to the Sun, not by axial tilt
error_signatures.example: Says summer happens because Earth is nearest the Sun

error_signatures.description: Cannot explain why the equator receives more concentrated energy than the poles
error_signatures.example: Says the poles get the same insolation as the equator

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: The equator gets concentrated, near-vertical sunlight (energy SURPLUS); the poles get slanted, spread-out sunlight (energy DEFICIT). Winds and ocean currents move heat from surplus to deficit areas — the energy balance. Seasons come from the 23,5° AXIAL TILT, not distance to the Sun.

atomic_skills.title: Global air circulation
atomic_skills.description: Global circulation as a response to unequal heating; world pressure belts; the tri-cellular model (Hadley, Ferrel and polar cells); the link between temperature, pressure and wind; pressure gradient, the Coriolis force and geostrophic flow; the global wind belts (westerlies, tropical and polar easterlies); and regional/local winds (monsoons, Föhn/berg).

error_signatures.description: Reverses the link between rising air and pressure
error_signatures.example: Says rising warm air creates high pressure

error_signatures.description: Gets the order or names of the three cells wrong
error_signatures.example: Places the polar cell at the equator

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Hot air RISES → LOW pressure (equator); cool air SINKS → HIGH pressure (about 30° and the poles). Three cells from equator to pole: HADLEY → FERREL → POLAR. The Coriolis force bends winds (right in the north, left in the south), creating the trade winds and westerlies.

atomic_skills.title: Africa's weather and climate
atomic_skills.description: Africa's climate regions; subsidence and convergence and their link to rainfall; the role of the surrounding oceans in controlling Africa's climate; the El Niño and La Niña processes and their effects on Africa; and reading synoptic weather maps over Africa.

error_signatures.description: Links subsidence (sinking air) to rain rather than to dry conditions
error_signatures.example: Says sinking air at 30° causes heavy rainfall

error_signatures.description: Swaps the typical effects of El Niño and La Niña on southern Africa
error_signatures.example: Says El Niño usually brings wetter conditions to southern Africa

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: CONVERGENCE (air meeting and rising) → rain (e.g. the equatorial belt). SUBSIDENCE (sinking air at ~30°) → dry deserts (Sahara, Kalahari). El Niño often brings DRIER, drought conditions to southern Africa; La Niña often brings WETTER conditions.

atomic_skills.title: Droughts and desertification
atomic_skills.description: Areas at risk at regional and local scales; the causes of drought; the causes of desertification; the effects of drought and desertification on people and the environment (including differences in vulnerability); and management strategies, with case studies.

error_signatures.description: Treats drought and desertification as the same thing
error_signatures.example: Says a single dry season is desertification

error_signatures.description: Sees desertification as purely natural, ignoring human causes like overgrazing
error_signatures.example: Says people cannot contribute to desertification

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: DROUGHT = a temporary period of below-normal rainfall. DESERTIFICATION = land permanently degrading to desert-like conditions, often from human pressure (overgrazing, deforestation, poor farming) ON TOP of dry climate. Manage with sustainable land use, reforestation, water harvesting and grazing control.

atomic_skills.title: Topography of horizontally layered rocks
atomic_skills.description: Landscapes formed on flat-lying rock — hilly landscapes, basaltic plateaus, canyon and Karoo landscapes (mesa, butte, conical hill); the concept of scarp retreat (back-wasting); and how people use these landscapes.

error_signatures.description: Cannot order mesa → butte → conical hill by size as erosion proceeds
error_signatures.example: Says a butte is larger than a mesa

error_signatures.description: Does not link these flat-topped landforms to a resistant cap rock
error_signatures.example: Says a mesa keeps its flat top with no hard rock layer

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Flat-lying hard 'cap rock' protects the softer rock below. As scarp retreat eats away the edges, a wide flat-topped MESA shrinks to a smaller flat-topped BUTTE, then to a CONICAL HILL once the cap is gone. Mesa > butte > conical hill.

atomic_skills.title: Topography of inclined/tilted strata
atomic_skills.description: Landforms on tilted rock layers — scarp slope and dip slope, cuesta, homoclinal ridge, hogsback, cuesta basin and cuesta dome; the processes that develop them; and how people use these landscapes.

error_signatures.description: Confuses the steep scarp slope with the gentle dip slope of a cuesta
error_signatures.example: Says the dip slope is the steeper side

error_signatures.description: Cannot distinguish cuesta, homoclinal ridge and hogsback by their angle of dip
error_signatures.example: Says a hogsback has a gentle dip slope like a cuesta

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: On tilted strata the GENTLE side following the rock dip is the DIP SLOPE; the STEEP cut-across side is the SCARP SLOPE. Steepness of dip tells the landform: gentle dip = CUESTA; moderate = HOMOCLINAL RIDGE; very steep/near-vertical = HOGSBACK.

atomic_skills.title: Topography of massive igneous rocks
atomic_skills.description: Identifying intrusive igneous bodies — batholiths, laccoliths, lopoliths, dykes and sills; and the characteristics and development of granite domes and tors.

error_signatures.description: Confuses a dyke (cuts across layers, vertical) with a sill (runs along layers, horizontal)
error_signatures.example: Says a sill cuts vertically across the rock layers

error_signatures.description: Thinks tors form by deposition rather than by weathering of jointed granite
error_signatures.example: Says tors are piles of rock dropped by rivers

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Intrusions: BATHOLITH = huge deep mass; LACCOLITH = dome-shaped, pushes layers up; LOPOLITH = saucer/basin shape; DYKE = cuts ACROSS layers (often vertical); SILL = runs ALONG (parallel to) layers. Tors are clusters of blocks left when jointed granite weathers and the loose material is removed.

atomic_skills.title: Slopes
atomic_skills.description: An overview of South Africa's topography; types of slopes; the slope elements — crest, cliff (free face/scarp), talus (scree/debris) and pediment — and their characteristics; how slopes develop over time; and the concept of slope retreat.

error_signatures.description: Cannot order the slope elements from top to bottom
error_signatures.example: Places the pediment above the cliff

error_signatures.description: Confuses talus (the loose rock) with the cliff that supplies it
error_signatures.example: Says the talus is the vertical rock face

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: From top to bottom: CREST (rounded top) → CLIFF / FREE FACE (steep bare rock) → TALUS / SCREE (loose broken rock piled below the cliff) → PEDIMENT (gentle rock surface at the base). Slope retreat means the whole slope moves back while keeping its shape.

atomic_skills.title: Mass movements & human responses
atomic_skills.description: The concept of mass movement; the main types — soil creep, solifluction, landslides, rockfalls, mudflows and slumps; their impact on people and the environment; and strategies to prevent or reduce their effects, with South African case studies.

error_signatures.description: Thinks all mass movements are fast and sudden, missing slow creep
error_signatures.example: Says soil creep happens in seconds like a rockfall

error_signatures.description: Ignores the role of water and gravity as triggers
error_signatures.example: Says heavy rain has no effect on landslides

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Mass movement = the downhill movement of rock/soil under GRAVITY. Speed varies: SOIL CREEP is very slow (millimetres a year); ROCKFALLS and LANDSLIDES are sudden and fast. Water often triggers them. Reduce risk with drainage, terracing, retaining walls, planting and avoiding building on unstable slopes.

atomic_skills.title: The concept of development
atomic_skills.description: Development terminology (developed/developing, MEDC/LEDC, industrialised); the meaning of development — economic, social, sustainable, appropriate-scale and spatial aspects; and the indicators used to measure it (GNP, GDP, HDI, Gini coefficient, life expectancy, infant mortality).

error_signatures.description: Reduces development to wealth alone, ignoring health, education and sustainability
error_signatures.example: Says a rich country is automatically fully developed

error_signatures.description: Misreads the HDI or Gini coefficient direction
error_signatures.example: Says a higher Gini coefficient means more equality

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Development is more than money: it includes health, education, equality and sustainability. HDI combines income, education and life expectancy (higher = more developed). The GINI coefficient measures inequality (higher = MORE unequal). Infant mortality FALLS as development rises.

atomic_skills.title: Frameworks for development
atomic_skills.description: Factors that affect development (resources, energy, history, trade imbalances, population growth, education, environmental degradation) and their inter-related nature; development models (free-market/Rostow with criticisms, core-periphery, sustainability models); and community-based rural and urban development.

error_signatures.description: Treats development factors as independent rather than inter-related
error_signatures.example: Says education has nothing to do with the economy

error_signatures.description: Cannot describe the core-periphery relationship
error_signatures.example: Says the periphery exploits the core

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Development factors interlink (e.g. poor education → low skills → weak economy → less money for schools). Rostow's model says countries pass through growth stages (criticised as too 'one path'). CORE-PERIPHERY: a wealthy CORE draws resources, money and people from a poorer PERIPHERY.

atomic_skills.title: Trade and development
atomic_skills.description: International trade and world markets (commodities and terms of trade); trading relationships — free trade, trade barriers, subsidies and fair trade; globalisation and its impact on development; and export-led development, critically examined.

error_signatures.description: Cannot explain why exporting raw materials and importing manufactured goods disadvantages a country
error_signatures.example: Says selling raw materials always makes a country rich

error_signatures.description: Confuses free trade, fair trade and trade barriers
error_signatures.example: Says fair trade means no rules at all

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Many developing countries export cheap RAW materials and import expensive MANUFACTURED goods — poor 'terms of trade' that keep them dependent. FREE TRADE = no barriers; TRADE BARRIERS = tariffs/quotas to protect local industry; FAIR TRADE = better prices and conditions for producers.

atomic_skills.title: Development issues and challenges
atomic_skills.description: The role of women in development (gender, power, access to resources and attitudes); the effect of development on the environment; and the role of the state and business in South African development (central state control, weak state control and public-private partnerships).

error_signatures.description: Overlooks how empowering women drives wider development
error_signatures.example: Says women's education has no effect on a country's development

error_signatures.description: Assumes economic development never harms the environment
error_signatures.example: Says growth and the environment never conflict

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Empowering women (education, jobs, rights, healthcare) lowers birth rates and lifts whole communities — a powerful development driver. Development can harm the environment (pollution, resource depletion), so it must be balanced. The state and business can lead development together via public-private partnerships.

atomic_skills.title: The role of development aid
atomic_skills.description: The concepts of development aid and development co-operation; types of aid — technical, conditional and humanitarian; and the positive and negative impacts of aid on development, with case studies.

error_signatures.description: Confuses the three aid types (technical, conditional, humanitarian)
error_signatures.example: Calls emergency disaster relief 'conditional aid'

error_signatures.description: Sees aid as only good or only bad, missing the trade-offs
error_signatures.example: Says aid always solves a country's problems

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: TECHNICAL aid = skills/expertise; CONDITIONAL aid = comes with strings attached (the receiver must do certain things); HUMANITARIAN aid = emergency relief after disasters. Aid can help (infrastructure, emergencies) BUT may create dependency, debt or serve the donor's interests — weigh both sides.

atomic_skills.title: Using resources
atomic_skills.description: The relationship between resources and economic development; the exploitation and depletion of resources; and the concepts of sustainability and sustainable use of resources.

error_signatures.description: Confuses renewable and non-renewable resources
error_signatures.example: Calls coal a renewable resource

error_signatures.description: Misunderstands sustainability as never using resources at all
error_signatures.example: Says sustainable use means using nothing

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: RENEWABLE resources replenish (sun, wind, water, forests if managed); NON-RENEWABLE resources run out (coal, oil, minerals). Sustainable use means meeting today's needs WITHOUT preventing future generations from meeting theirs — use wisely, not not at all.

atomic_skills.title: Soil and soil erosion
atomic_skills.description: How soils form; soil as a resource; the human, animal and physical causes of soil erosion (past and present); evidence of soil erosion in South Africa; its effects on people and the environment; and strategies to prevent and control it.

error_signatures.description: Sees soil erosion as purely natural, ignoring overgrazing and poor farming
error_signatures.example: Says people cannot cause soil erosion

error_signatures.description: Confuses sheet, rill, gully (donga) and wind erosion
error_signatures.example: Calls a deep gully 'sheet erosion'

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Soil forms slowly from weathered rock + organic matter — it is a precious, slow-to-replace resource. Erosion is sped up by overgrazing, ploughing, deforestation and bare soil. Types: SHEET (thin layer), RILL (small channels), GULLY/DONGA (deep). Control with contour ploughing, terracing, cover crops and managed grazing.

atomic_skills.title: Conventional energy sources
atomic_skills.description: Thermal, hydro and nuclear energy production in South Africa; coal-based thermal generation (principles and processes); the environmental impact of coal mining and power stations (despoliation, solid waste, waste gases, acid rain); a nuclear case study; and South Africa's long-term conventional energy potential.

error_signatures.description: Does not know coal dominates South Africa's electricity supply
error_signatures.example: Says most SA electricity comes from nuclear power

error_signatures.description: Overlooks the environmental costs of coal (acid rain, CO₂)
error_signatures.example: Says burning coal has no environmental impact

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: South Africa relies heavily on COAL-fired thermal power (cheap, abundant, but high CO₂, air pollution, acid rain and ash). Nuclear (Koeberg) gives steady, low-carbon power but raises waste and safety concerns. Conventional sources are reliable but non-renewable and polluting.

atomic_skills.title: Non-conventional energy sources
atomic_skills.description: Solar and wind energy with examples from South Africa and the world; the future of non-conventional energy in South Africa; and the possible effects of using more non-conventional energy on the economy and the environment.

error_signatures.description: Thinks renewables have no drawbacks at all
error_signatures.example: Says solar power works equally well at night

error_signatures.description: Does not recognise South Africa's strong solar and wind potential
error_signatures.example: Says South Africa has poor solar resources

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: South Africa has excellent SOLAR (sunny interior) and WIND (coastal) potential. Renewables are clean and inexhaustible BUT can be intermittent (no sun at night, variable wind), need storage, and have upfront costs and land/visual impacts. They cut emissions and create new industries and jobs.

atomic_skills.title: Energy management in South Africa
atomic_skills.description: South Africa's changing energy needs; and energy management towards greener economies and sustainable lifestyles — the responsibilities of governments, businesses and individuals.

error_signatures.description: Thinks only the government is responsible for energy management
error_signatures.example: Says individuals can do nothing to save energy

error_signatures.description: Confuses energy efficiency (using less for the same task) with simply going without
error_signatures.example: Says efficiency means switching everything off permanently

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Managing energy is a SHARED responsibility: governments (policy, renewables, grid), businesses (efficient processes, cleaner tech) and individuals (saving electricity, efficient appliances). Energy EFFICIENCY means getting the same result using LESS energy — a key route to a greener economy.

levels.title: Grade 12 — Geography
levels.description: Climate & weather (mid-latitude and tropical cyclones, subtropical anticyclones, valley and urban climates). Geomorphology (drainage systems, fluvial processes, catchment management). Settlement (rural and urban settlement, hierarchies, structure and issues). Economic geography of South Africa (economic structure, agriculture, mining, secondary/tertiary, industrial development, informal sector). Plus the mapwork strand. 23 atomic skills, all unlocked, learner-chosen order.

atomic_skills.title: Synoptic & topographic map techniques
atomic_skills.description: Reading synoptic weather maps and satellite-image data; grid referencing; direction with magnetic north, true north and magnetic declination; gradient; contours and cross-sections; and intervisibility — all from values given in the question.

error_signatures.description: Applies magnetic declination in the wrong direction when converting bearings
error_signatures.example: Subtracts a western declination instead of adding it

error_signatures.description: Confuses true north, magnetic north and grid north
error_signatures.example: Says a compass points to true north

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Magnetic bearing = true bearing + magnetic declination (for a western declination). A compass points to MAGNETIC north, which drifts over time. Read synoptic maps in order: pressure cells → isobar spacing (wind) → station data → overall weather.

atomic_skills.title: GIS & photo interpretation
atomic_skills.description: Interpreting vertical aerial photos and orthophoto maps and comparing them with topographic maps; and GIS concepts — remote sensing and resolution, spatial vs attribute data, raster vs vector, data standardisation/sharing/security, and data manipulation (integration, buffering, querying, statistical analysis).

error_signatures.description: Confuses GIS operations such as buffering and querying
error_signatures.example: Says buffering means deleting data

error_signatures.description: Mixes up spatial data (where) and attribute data (what)
error_signatures.example: Says attribute data is the map's coordinates

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: GIS stores SPATIAL data (where things are) and ATTRIBUTE data (facts about them) in layers. BUFFERING = a zone around a feature (e.g. 500 m around a river); QUERYING = asking the data a question to select features; data INTEGRATION = combining layers. An orthophoto is corrected to true scale, so it can be measured like a map.

atomic_skills.title: Mid-latitude cyclones
atomic_skills.description: General characteristics and where mid-latitude cyclones form; the conditions needed; the stages of development and their weather; the weather of cold, warm and occluded fronts; and reading satellite images and synoptic maps.

error_signatures.description: Swaps the weather of a cold front and a warm front
error_signatures.example: Says the warm front brings sudden heavy thunderstorms and gusty cold air

error_signatures.description: Does not link mid-latitude cyclones to the westerlies / 30–60° belts
error_signatures.example: Says mid-latitude cyclones form at the equator

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Mid-latitude cyclones form at ~30–60° where warm and cold air meet (the westerlies). A COLD front = steep, sudden heavy rain then colder, clearer air. A WARM front = gentle, prolonged lighter rain then warmer air. An OCCLUDED front is where the cold front catches the warm front. They affect the Western Cape in winter.

atomic_skills.title: Tropical cyclones
atomic_skills.description: General characteristics and where tropical cyclones form; the factors needed for formation; their stages of development and weather; reading satellite/synoptic data; a southern-African case study; their impact on people and the environment; and preparation and management strategies.

error_signatures.description: Thinks tropical cyclones form over land or cold water
error_signatures.example: Says a tropical cyclone strengthens once it moves over land

error_signatures.description: Confuses the calm 'eye' with the destructive eye wall
error_signatures.example: Says the strongest winds are in the eye

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Tropical cyclones need WARM ocean water (≥ 26–27 °C), so they form over tropical seas and WEAKEN over land or cold water. The EYE is calm and clear; the EYE WALL around it has the strongest winds and heaviest rain. They bring extreme wind, rain, flooding and storm surge (e.g. Cyclone Idai).

atomic_skills.title: Subtropical anticyclones & South Africa's weather
atomic_skills.description: The high-pressure cells affecting South Africa (South Atlantic, South Indian, Kalahari highs); their general characteristics; anticyclonic circulation and its influence on weather and climate; travelling disturbances (moisture front, line thunderstorms, coastal lows, berg winds); and reading the related synoptic maps.

error_signatures.description: Cannot explain why berg winds are hot and dry
error_signatures.example: Says berg winds bring cold, wet weather to the coast

error_signatures.description: Names the wrong high-pressure cells around South Africa
error_signatures.example: Says a low-pressure cell sits permanently over the Kalahari in winter

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Three highs steer SA's weather: the South Atlantic HP (west), South Indian HP (east) and the Kalahari/continental HP (interior, strong in winter). Anticyclonic (sinking) air brings dry, stable weather. BERG WINDS blow from the interior to the coast, warming and drying as they descend — hot, dry coastal conditions.

atomic_skills.title: Valley climates
atomic_skills.description: The micro-climate of valleys and the effect of slope aspect; the development of anabatic and katabatic winds, temperature inversions, frost pockets and radiation fog; and the influence of these local climates on settlement and farming.

error_signatures.description: Swaps anabatic (upslope, day) and katabatic (downslope, night) winds
error_signatures.example: Says katabatic winds blow up the valley during the day

error_signatures.description: Cannot link katabatic flow to frost pockets at the valley floor
error_signatures.example: Says the coldest night air collects on the hilltops

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: ANABATIC winds blow UP-slope by DAY (warm air rises). KATABATIC winds drain cold dense air DOWN-slope at NIGHT, pooling on the valley floor → temperature INVERSION, FROST POCKETS and radiation fog at the bottom. Farmers plant frost-sensitive crops on the warmer mid-slopes, not the cold floor.

atomic_skills.title: Urban climates
atomic_skills.description: Why urban and rural climates differ; the urban heat island — its causes and effects; pollution domes — their causes and effects; and strategies to reduce the heat-island effect.

error_signatures.description: Thinks cities are cooler than surrounding countryside
error_signatures.example: Says the city centre is the coolest part of a region

error_signatures.description: Cannot link concrete, tar and waste heat to the heat-island effect
error_signatures.example: Says building materials have no effect on city temperature

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Cities are WARMER than the countryside (the urban HEAT ISLAND): dark concrete and tar absorb heat, buildings block wind, and cars, factories and air-conditioners release waste heat. A POLLUTION DOME traps dirty air over the city. Reduce it with parks, trees, green roofs and lighter, reflective surfaces.

atomic_skills.title: Drainage systems in South Africa
atomic_skills.description: Key concepts (drainage basin, catchment, watershed, tributary, confluence, source, mouth, water table, run-off, groundwater); types of rivers (permanent, periodic, episodic, exotic); drainage patterns (dendritic, trellis, rectangular, radial, centripetal, deranged, parallel); drainage density and stream order; and laminar vs turbulent flow.

error_signatures.description: Confuses watershed (the dividing high ground) with the river itself
error_signatures.example: Says the watershed is the main river channel

error_signatures.description: Cannot match a drainage pattern to its underlying rock structure
error_signatures.example: Says a trellis pattern forms on uniform flat rock

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: A DRAINAGE BASIN/CATCHMENT is all the land drained by one river system; the WATERSHED is the high ground dividing basins. Patterns reflect the rock: DENDRITIC (tree-like) on uniform rock; TRELLIS (rectangular branching) on alternating hard/soft tilted rock; RADIAL (outward) off a dome/mountain; CENTRIPETAL (inward) into a basin.

atomic_skills.title: Fluvial processes & landforms
atomic_skills.description: Transverse and longitudinal river profiles and river stages; fluvial landforms (meanders, oxbow lakes, braided streams, floodplains, natural levees, waterfalls, rapids, deltas); river grading; rejuvenation features (knickpoints, terraces, incised meanders); river capture/stream piracy; and superimposed and antecedent drainage.

error_signatures.description: Confuses upper-course features (V-valleys, waterfalls) with lower-course features (meanders, deltas)
error_signatures.example: Says deltas form in the upper course

error_signatures.description: Cannot explain how an oxbow lake forms from a meander
error_signatures.example: Says oxbow lakes form on straight river sections

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: UPPER course = steep, fast, eroding: V-shaped valleys, waterfalls, rapids. LOWER course = gentle, depositing: meanders, oxbow lakes, floodplains, levees, deltas. An OXBOW LAKE forms when a looping meander is cut off and abandoned. Rejuvenation (renewed erosion) gives knickpoints, river terraces and incised meanders.

atomic_skills.title: Catchment & river management
atomic_skills.description: Why managing drainage basins and catchments matters; the impact of people on catchments; and a South African catchment-management case study.

error_signatures.description: Treats upstream and downstream as unconnected
error_signatures.example: Says pollution upstream does not affect downstream users

error_signatures.description: Overlooks how alien vegetation or farming affects water yield
error_signatures.example: Says clearing alien trees has no effect on river flow

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: A catchment is one connected system — what happens upstream (pollution, farming, alien plants, building) affects everyone downstream. Good management protects water QUALITY and QUANTITY: control pollution, clear water-hungry alien plants, protect wetlands and coordinate users across the whole basin.

atomic_skills.title: Study of settlements
atomic_skills.description: The concept of settlement; site versus situation; rural and urban settlements; and classifying settlements by size, complexity, pattern and function.

error_signatures.description: Confuses site (the actual land a settlement is built on) with situation (its position relative to other places)
error_signatures.example: Says 'near a major road junction' describes the site

error_signatures.description: Cannot classify a settlement by function
error_signatures.example: Says all settlements have the same function

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: SITE = the actual ground a settlement stands on (flat land, near water, defensible). SITUATION = where it sits in relation to other places (on routes, near resources, central). Settlements are classified by SIZE, PATTERN (shape), and FUNCTION (what they mainly do — mining, port, market).

atomic_skills.title: Rural settlements
atomic_skills.description: How site and situation affect the location of rural settlements; classifying them by pattern and function; reasons for different shapes (round, linear, T-shaped, cross-road); and land use in rural settlements.

error_signatures.description: Confuses nucleated (clustered) and dispersed (scattered) rural patterns
error_signatures.example: Calls scattered farmsteads a 'nucleated' settlement

error_signatures.description: Cannot link a settlement shape to its cause (e.g. linear along a road or river)
error_signatures.example: Says a linear village forms for no reason

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: NUCLEATED = houses clustered together (often around water or a crossroads); DISPERSED = scattered farmsteads. Shapes follow the cause: LINEAR along a road/river/valley; CROSS-ROAD or T-SHAPED at route junctions; ROUND/clustered around a central point like a water source.

atomic_skills.title: Rural settlement issues
atomic_skills.description: Rural-urban migration; the causes and consequences of rural depopulation for people and the economy; a case study of depopulation and responses; and social-justice issues in rural areas (access to resources and land reform).

error_signatures.description: Confuses depopulation (loss of people) with overpopulation
error_signatures.example: Says rural depopulation means too many people in the countryside

error_signatures.description: Misses that mostly young, able adults leave, ageing the rural population
error_signatures.example: Says depopulation removes mainly the elderly

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Rural DEPOPULATION = the countryside losing people, mainly young working-age adults moving to cities for jobs and services. This leaves an ageing population, labour shortages, closed schools/shops and weakened local economies. Land reform and rural development aim to address the inequalities that drive it.

atomic_skills.title: Urban settlements
atomic_skills.description: The origin and development of urban settlements and the urbanisation of the world's population; how site and situation affect urban location; and classifying urban settlements by function (central places, trade/transport, break-of-bulk points, specialised cities, junction and gateway/gap towns).

error_signatures.description: Cannot explain a break-of-bulk point
error_signatures.example: Says a break-of-bulk point is where a city runs out of land

error_signatures.description: Confuses urban function types (port, junction, gateway)
error_signatures.example: Calls an inland mining town a 'port city'

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Urban FUNCTION = a town's main job: PORT/break-of-bulk (where goods change transport, e.g. ship to rail), JUNCTION (route crossing), GATEWAY/GAP (controls a route through a barrier), SPECIALISED (mining, university, resort), CENTRAL PLACE (services for a surrounding area).

atomic_skills.title: Urban hierarchies
atomic_skills.description: The concepts of urban hierarchy, central place, threshold population, sphere of influence and range of goods; lower- and higher-order functions and services; and lower- and higher-order centres.

error_signatures.description: Swaps low-order and high-order goods/services
error_signatures.example: Calls a daily loaf of bread a high-order good

error_signatures.description: Cannot link threshold population to range of goods
error_signatures.example: Says a small village can support a specialist hospital

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: LOW-ORDER goods/services are cheap, bought often, with a small THRESHOLD and short RANGE (bread, spaza shop) — found in many small centres. HIGH-ORDER goods are expensive, bought rarely, needing a large threshold and long range (specialist hospital, university) — found only in a few large cities. Hence the hierarchy: many small centres, few big ones.

atomic_skills.title: Urban structure & patterns
atomic_skills.description: The internal structure of cities — land-use zones, the urban profile, and factors shaping a city's morphology; models of urban structure (multiple-nuclei, modern Western city, Third-World city, South African city); and changing urban patterns and land use in South African cities.

error_signatures.description: Cannot identify the CBD or explain its characteristics
error_signatures.example: Says the CBD has the lowest land values and tallest trees

error_signatures.description: Misses how apartheid shaped the South African city model
error_signatures.example: Says South African cities developed exactly like American ones

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: The CBD (central business district) has the highest land values, tallest buildings and best accessibility. Land value generally FALLS outwards. The SOUTH AFRICAN city is distinctive: apartheid planning placed townships and 'buffer zones' that separated communities — patterns that still shape cities today.

atomic_skills.title: Urban settlement issues
atomic_skills.description: Recent urbanisation patterns in South Africa; issues from rapid urbanisation (poor planning, housing shortages, overcrowding, traffic congestion, service problems); the growth of informal settlements; and case studies of how SA urban areas manage environmental, economic and social-justice challenges.

error_signatures.description: Blames informal settlements on residents rather than housing shortages and inequality
error_signatures.example: Says informal settlements exist because people refuse formal housing

error_signatures.description: Cannot connect rapid urbanisation to its service and infrastructure pressures
error_signatures.example: Says fast city growth causes no service problems

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Rapid urbanisation outpaces housing and services, producing INFORMAL SETTLEMENTS, overcrowding, traffic and strained water/sanitation. The cause is structural — too little affordable housing and deep inequality — not personal choice. Responses include upgrading settlements, integrated housing and better transport and services.

tiers.title: Term 3 — Economic Geography of South Africa

atomic_skills.title: Structure of the economy
atomic_skills.description: The economic sectors (primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary); their contribution to the South African economy by value and employment; and the use of statistical and graphical information.

error_signatures.description: Misclassifies activities into the wrong economic sector
error_signatures.example: Calls a car factory a primary-sector activity

error_signatures.description: Cannot read sector contribution from a graph or table
error_signatures.example: Says the largest sector by employment must be the largest by value

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: PRIMARY = extracting raw materials (farming, mining, fishing). SECONDARY = making/manufacturing (factories). TERTIARY = services (shops, banks, transport). QUATERNARY = knowledge/research (IT, R&D). In South Africa the tertiary sector dominates GDP; sectors can differ in their share of VALUE versus EMPLOYMENT.

atomic_skills.title: Agriculture
atomic_skills.description: Agriculture's contribution to the economy; the role of small-scale and large-scale farmers; main products for home and export markets; factors that favour and hinder farming (climate, soil, land ownership, trade); and food security in South Africa, with case studies.

error_signatures.description: Confuses food security with simply producing lots of food
error_signatures.example: Says a country with big farms automatically has food security

error_signatures.description: Overlooks how limited water/arable land constrains SA farming
error_signatures.example: Says climate and water never limit South African agriculture

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: FOOD SECURITY = all people having reliable ACCESS to enough safe, nutritious food — it depends on availability, affordability AND access, not just total production. SA farming is limited by low, variable rainfall and limited arable land, and shaped by the history of land ownership; large commercial and small-scale farmers play different roles.

atomic_skills.title: Mining
atomic_skills.description: Mining's contribution to the economy; its significance for South Africa's development; the factors that favour and hinder mining; and a case study of one major South African mineral.

error_signatures.description: Sees mining as only beneficial, ignoring its environmental and social costs
error_signatures.example: Says mining has no downside for communities or the environment

error_signatures.description: Misses the risk of depending on a finite, price-volatile resource
error_signatures.example: Says mineral income will last forever and never changes

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: Mining built South Africa's economy (gold, platinum, coal, diamonds) — earning foreign exchange and jobs. BUT minerals are FINITE and prices swing; mining also causes environmental damage (acid mine drainage, dust, land), health risks and reliance on a single sector. Diversifying the economy reduces this risk.

atomic_skills.title: Secondary & tertiary sectors
atomic_skills.description: The contribution of the secondary and tertiary sectors; types of industry (heavy, light, raw-material- vs market-oriented, footloose, ubiquitous, bridge/break-of-bulk); factors influencing industrial location; and South Africa's main industrial regions (Gauteng/PWV, Durban-Pinetown, PE-Uitenhage, SW Cape).

error_signatures.description: Confuses raw-material-oriented and market-oriented industries
error_signatures.example: Says a heavy steel works should locate far from its raw materials

error_signatures.description: Cannot define a footloose industry
error_signatures.example: Says a footloose industry must be near a mine

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: RAW-MATERIAL-oriented industries (heavy, bulky inputs that lose weight, e.g. steel) locate near the raw material; MARKET-oriented industries (products bulky/perishable, e.g. bread) locate near customers. FOOTLOOSE industries (e.g. electronics, IT) can locate almost anywhere. Gauteng (PWV) is SA's largest industrial region.

atomic_skills.title: Strategies for industrial development
atomic_skills.description: Apartheid and post-apartheid industrial-development strategies; the concept and distribution of Industrial Development Zones (IDZs); case studies of Spatial Development Initiatives (SDIs, e.g. the Maputo Corridor); and the issues of industrial centralisation versus decentralisation.

error_signatures.description: Confuses centralisation and decentralisation of industry
error_signatures.example: Says decentralisation means concentrating industry in one big city

error_signatures.description: Cannot explain the purpose of an IDZ or SDI
error_signatures.example: Says an SDI is a type of mineral

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: DECENTRALISATION spreads industry AWAY from crowded cores to develop poorer regions and ease congestion; CENTRALISATION concentrates it for shared infrastructure and markets. IDZs offer incentives to attract export industry (often near ports); SDIs (e.g. the Maputo Development Corridor) develop transport routes to unlock a region's economic potential.

atomic_skills.title: Informal sector
atomic_skills.description: The concept and characteristics of informal-sector employment; the reasons for high informal-sector employment in South Africa; and the challenges facing the sector, with South African case studies.

error_signatures.description: Cannot distinguish formal- and informal-sector work
error_signatures.example: Says a street vendor pays company tax and has a formal contract

error_signatures.description: Sees the informal sector as unimportant rather than a vital source of income
error_signatures.example: Says the informal sector provides no benefit to the economy

atomic_skills.recovery_strategy: The INFORMAL sector is unregistered, untaxed, small-scale work (street vendors, spaza shops, casual labour) — no contracts, benefits or job security. It is large in South Africa because of high unemployment and limited formal jobs. It provides vital income and goods but faces low pay, insecurity and little legal protection.
